title: The vow of food, the meditations on Brahman, and the song of the one who knows
theme: The Bhṛguvallī ends with a vow never to turn away a guest, a list of the names under which Brahman is to be meditated on in the body and in nature, and the knower who has passed through the five selves singing that he is food, the eater of food and the one who joins them.

words.context: kam-cana, ‘any one whatever’ — Kūranārāyaṇa: even an outcaste («आचण्डालं»)

words.role: locative of occasion: ‘for a night’s lodging’
words.context: Śaṅkara: «वसतिनिमित्तं», for the sake of a place to stay

words.role: with yayā: ‘by any means at all’
completes yayā kayā ca, ‘by any whatsoever’
verb of the quoted words: ‘[food] is ready’
main verb; its subject is ‘the knowers’ (Śaṅkara: «अन्नवन्तो विद्वांसः»)

words.meaning: from the front: first, or in the best way
words.context: Śaṅkara: «मुख्ये प्रथमे वयसि मुख्यया वा वृत्त्या», in the first part of life, or in the best manner

words.role: adverb: the return matches the gift
adverb: in middle life, or with middling care (Śaṅkara)
adverb: in old age, or grudgingly (Śaṅkara)

sandhi.type: final t before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: t becomes d before the v of vratam, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).
u before a dissimilar vowel becomes v, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).

arādhi asmai: i becomes y, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि). asmai annam: ai becomes āy before the vowel, P. 6.1.78 (एचोऽयवायावः), and the y is dropped, P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य); the hiatus that results is the rule’s own.
The visarga of -taḥ becomes u before a, P. 6.1.113 (अतो रोरप्लुतादप्लुते); a + u gives o, and the following a is absorbed into it, P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति), written with avagraha.

sandhi.type: ai before a vowel; aḥ before a
sandhi.rule: vai before a: ai becomes āy, P. 6.1.78 (एचोऽयवायावः), and the y is dropped, P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य). antataḥ annam: as in mukhato ’nnam.

morphology.note: Passive aorist (‘it has been made ready’) of rādh; Śaṅkara glosses it «अराधि संसिद्धम्». The words are what the knowers say to the guest at the door.

The suffix -tas makes an adverb of mukha, ‘mouth, front’: ‘from the front’. Śaṅkara gives two senses together, ‘in the first part of life’ and ‘in the foremost manner’, and the same pair for madhyataḥ and antataḥ.
Present passive of rādh, ‘is accomplished, comes to’; it answers the participle rāddham of the line before: food given thus comes back thus.

translation.literal: Not anyone [who comes] for lodging should one turn away. That [is the] vow. Therefore by whatever means one should obtain much food. ‘Food has been made ready for him’ — thus they say. This food indeed [given] in the first way, for him in the first way food comes. This [given] in the middle way, for him in the middle way food comes. This [given] in the last way, for him in the last way food comes.
translation.readable: Never turn away anyone who asks to stay; that is the vow. So get plenty of food by whatever means you can: the wise say to the guest, “Food is ready for you.” Food given in the first and best way returns to the giver in the first and best way; given in the middling way, it returns in the middling way; given in the last and meanest way, it returns in the last way.

words.role: verb of the relative clause; its main clause is understood (‘to him it comes so’)
the name under which [Brahman] is meditated
words.context: Śaṅkara: «क्षेमो नाम उपात्तपरिरक्षणम्», keeping what one has
Śaṅkara: yoga is gaining what one has not («योगः अनुपात्तस्योपादानम्»)

sandhi.type: aḥ before a vowel other than a
sandhi.rule: The visarga becomes y before a vowel, P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), and the y is dropped, P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य); the hiatus kṣema iti is the rule’s.
A visarga after i or u goes back to r before a vowel: gatir iti.

samasa.meaning: gaining and keeping. The singular is noted by the commentators: Kūranārāyaṇa explains it by an elided middle member («मध्यमपदलोपिसमासेन उभयोपदेशात् एकवचनम्»), Govindarāja calls the treatment as one Vedic («एकवद्भावे पुल्लिङ्गश्छान्दसः»).
in-breath and out-breath; Kūranārāyaṇa pairs them with gaining and keeping, breath for gaining («तद्धेतुः प्राणः»), out-breath for keeping

morphology.note: From sam-ā-jñā, ‘to know together, to designate’: names under which a thing is to be known. Śaṅkara takes them as meditations («उपासनानीत्यर्थः»).
Vedic nominative plural feminine in -īḥ (classical daivyaḥ); Śaṅkara restates it as «दैव्यः».

translation.literal: Who knows thus [— to him it comes so]. ‘Keeping’ — thus in speech. ‘Gaining and keeping’ — thus in in-breath and out-breath. ‘Action’ — thus in the hands. ‘Movement’ — thus in the feet. ‘Release’ — thus in the anus. Thus the human designations. Now the divine: ‘satisfaction’ — thus in rain. ‘Strength’ — thus in lightning.
translation.readable: For one who knows this, it is so. [Meditate on Brahman] as keeping, in speech; as gaining and keeping, in the breaths; as action, in the hands; as movement, in the feet; as release, in the organ of excretion. These are the meditations within the person. Now those among the powers of nature: as satisfaction, in rain; as strength, in lightning —

words.context: Śaṅkara: immortality through a son, by release from the debt to the ancestors («पुत्रेण ऋणविमोक्षद्वारेण»)
Śaṅkara: the Brahman just spoken of; Govindarāja: space («सर्वत्र तच्छब्दात् आकाशम् उच्यते»)

words.role: name under which it is meditated

words.meaning: possessed of a foundation, well established

words.context: Śaṅkara: «मननसमर्थो भवति», able to think; Kūranārāyaṇa: «आनन्दाभिमानवान् भवति»

sandhi.type: iḥ before a vowel; m before a vowel; aḥ before i; yaṇ
sandhi.rule: prajātir: visarga after i is r before a vowel. amṛtam ānandaḥ: final m joins the vowel. ānanda iti: aḥ before i loses its visarga with hiatus, P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य). ity upasthe: P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).
ā + i → e, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः); i before u becomes y, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).

sandhi.type: t before a nasal; aḥ before i
sandhi.rule: tat before m may become n (tan mahaḥ); mahaḥ before i loses its visarga with hiatus.

morphology.note: Possessive -vat: ‘one who has a foundation’. The pattern holds through the list — meditate on it as X, become X-vat — which Śaṅkara grounds in a śruti he cites: «तं यथा यथोपासते तदेव भवति».
Possessive -vat of māna (from man, ‘think’ or ‘honour’). Śaṅkara: «मननसमर्थो भवति»; Kūranārāyaṇa takes māna as esteem (‘mana’ as «बहुमानः वा»).

translation.literal: ‘Fame’ — thus in cattle. ‘Light’ — thus in the stars. ‘Procreation, immortality, joy’ — thus in the organ of generation. ‘All’ — thus in space. As ‘foundation’ one should meditate on that; one becomes well founded. As ‘greatness’ one should meditate on that; one becomes great. As ‘mind’ one should meditate on that; one becomes thoughtful.
translation.readable: — as fame, in cattle; as light, in the stars; as procreation, immortality and joy, in the organ of generation; as the whole, in space. Meditate on it as the foundation, and you are well founded; as greatness, and you become great; as mind, and you become able to think.

words.meaning: the dying-round, that in which [all] die
words.context: Śaṅkara: in it the five deities die («परिम्रियन्तेऽस्मिन्पञ्च देवता»), hence the wind

sandhi.rule: The initial a after final e is absorbed, P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति), written with avagraha.
i before e becomes y, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).
The visarga becomes ś before c, P. 8.4.40 (स्तोः श्चुना श्चुः) after its change to s; ca ayam → cāyam, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).

morphology.note: enam with Vedic ṇ: Raṅgarāmānuja «पर्येणम् इति णत्वं छान्दसम्». The preverb pari stands apart from its verb mriyante (tmesis) and is repeated in the next line.

From pari-mṛ, ‘to die around’: ‘that in which [things] die’. Śaṅkara identifies it as the wind, the five deities lightning, rain, moon, sun and fire dying into it, and the wind as one with space; Raṅgarāmānuja, as space, the place of all dying («परितः म्रियन्ते अस्मिन् इति परिमरः»).
Derived from bhrātṛ, ‘brother’: the rival among one’s own kin. Śaṅkara distinguishes those who hate from rivals who do not («अद्विषन्तोऽपि»).

translation.literal: As ‘homage’ one should meditate on that; desires bow down to him. As ‘Brahman’ one should meditate on that; one becomes possessed of Brahman. As ‘the dying-around of Brahman’ one should meditate on that; around him die hating rivals, around [him die] the rivals who are unfriendly. And he who is in the person, and he who is in the sun — he is one.
translation.readable: Meditate on it as homage, and what you desire bows to you; as Brahman, the vast, and you become vast. Meditate on it as that in which all dies, and around you your hating rivals die, and the kinsmen who wish you ill. The one in the person and the one in the sun are one.

words.role: subject, taken up by the participles

words.context: Bhāradvāja: «तत्समीपं गत्वा तेन सङ्गतः»; Śaṅkara takes it of passing through each self in turn

sandhi.rule: t becomes l before l, P. 8.4.60 (तोर्लि).
Final n before l becomes a nasalised l, written here with anusvāra and ll (imāṃl lokān); the Sāyaṇa-pāṭha and Madhva’s text spell the nasal differently (corrections.json).
A final n after a short vowel is doubled before a vowel, P. 8.3.32 (ङमो ह्रस्वादचि ङमुण्नित्यम्).

samasa.meaning: taking forms at will (Śaṅkara: «कामतो रूपाण्यस्येति कामरूपी»)

morphology.note: A stobha, a syllable of the sāman chant without lexical meaning; the 3 marks pluta. Śaṅkara: an exclamation of wonder, ‘aho!’. Kūranārāyaṇa derives it from ho with the pluti of P. 8.2.107 (एचोऽप्रगृह्यस्यादूराद्धूते पूर्वस्यार्धस्यादुत्तरस्येदुतौ), which splits the diphthong (that is his citation). Raṅgarāmānuja calls them stobha syllables («स्तोभाक्षराणि»).

Gerund of upa-sam-kram, repeated five times. Whether it means ‘passing beyond’ each self (Śaṅkara) or ‘coming near to’ the self of bliss as to another (Bhāradvāja, Kūranārāyaṇa) is the main question of this unit.

translation.literal: He who knows thus, having departed from this world, having passed into this self made of food, having passed into this self made of breath, having passed into this self made of mind, having passed into this self made of understanding, having passed into this self made of bliss, moving through these worlds, eating at will, taking form at will, sits singing this sāman: hā3vu, hā3vu, hā3vu!
translation.readable: One who knows this, leaving this world, passes into the self made of food, into the self made of breath, of mind, of understanding, and into the self made of bliss. Then, moving through these worlds, with food at will and form at will, he sits and sings this chant: “Ah! Ah! Ah!”

words.meaning: maker of the joining (or: of what is praised)
words.context: Śaṅkara: «श्लोको नाम अन्नान्नादयोः सङ्घातः»; Govindarāja: «श्लोककृत् पद्यकृत् दासभूतः»

words.role: dependent on prathamajāḥ; ṛtasya with its a prolated

words.context: Raṅgarāmānuja: «नाभा इ इति गानकृतः विकारः», a change made by the chant
Raṅgarāmānuja: «इच्छब्दोऽनर्थकः», without meaning of its own
Śaṅkara: «आवा अवतीत्यर्थः»; Raṅgarāmānuja from vā, ‘to go’ («वा गतिगन्धनयो:»)

words.role: object of ādmi: ‘the one eating food’
main verb; admi with its a prolated

sandhi.rule: annādaḥ before aham: the visarga becomes u, P. 6.1.113 (अतो रोरप्लुतादप्लुते), a + u → o, and the a of aham is absorbed, P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति). The chant then prolates the o (annādo3); the prolation is the singer’s, not a change of the word.
t becomes d before a vowel, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).
The visarga becomes u before the voiced m, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च); a + u → o.
mā + āvāḥ → māvāḥ, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः); the chant prolates the long ā (mā3vāḥ).
suvaḥ is a word whose visarga goes back to r; the r stays before the voiced n.

morphology.note: jan + the suffix viṭ, whose nasal becomes ā: Kūranārāyaṇa and Govindarāja cite P. 3.2.67 (जनसनखनक्रमगमो विट्) and P. 6.4.41 (विड्वनोरनुनासिकस्यात्‌) (their citations). The nominative is masculine prathamajāḥ; the text has ‘prathamajā’ before the vowel of ṛtasya.
ṛtasya with its second vowel prolated in the chant (ṛtā3sya); the word is the genitive of ṛta.

The chant’s form of nābhiḥ, ‘navel’: Raṅgarāmānuja calls it a change made by singing («नाभा इ इति गानकृतः विकारः»), and Rāmānanda the same («विकृतगानप्रयुक्ता»). The padaccheda keeps the sung form; Śaṅkara glosses «अमृतस्य नाभिः».

A Vedic form without a classical equivalent. Śaṅkara: «आवा अवतीत्यर्थः», ‘he protects [me]’, from av; Raṅgarāmānuja and Rāmānanda derive it from vā, ‘to go’ (‘he reaches me’); Govindarāja calls it a Vedic subjunctive («लेटि छान्दसं रूपम्»).
admi, ‘I eat’, with its first vowel prolated in the chant.

abhyabhavam, imperfect first person of abhi-bhū, prolated at the end. Śaṅkara gives it a present sense («अभिभवामि»); Kūranārāyaṇa reads a Vedic subjunctive with āṭ, ‘may I overcome’, citing P. 3.4.94 (लेटोऽडाटौ) (his citation).
jyotiḥ with a Vedic long ī.

translation.literal: I [am] food, I [am] food, I [am] food. I [am] the eater of food, I [am] the eater of food, I [am] the eater of food. I [am] the maker of the śloka, I [am] the maker of the śloka, I [am] the maker of the śloka. I am the first-born of the true order, before the gods, the navel of immortality. Who gives me, he indeed protects me. I, food, eat the one eating food. I have overcome the whole world. [My] light [is] like the sun. Who knows thus. Thus the Upaniṣad.
translation.readable: “I am food! I am food! I am food! I am the eater of food! I am the eater of food! I am the eater of food! I am the one who joins them! I am the one who joins them! I am the one who joins them! I am the first-born of the true order, older than the gods, the centre of immortality. Whoever gives me away preserves me; whoever eats food without giving, I, food, eat him. I have overcome the whole world; my light is like the sun.” So it is for one who knows this. This is the Upaniṣad.

syntax: The anuvāka is prose in short clauses. Unit 1 is a prohibition in the optative (na … pratyācakṣīta), a statement (tad vratam), an injunction (prāpnuyāt) and a quoted saying (arādhy asmā annam iti), followed by three parallel pairs: ‘this food [given] mukhataḥ … mukhataḥ for him food comes’. Units 2–4 are a list of the form ‘X iti [locus in the locative]’, with upāsīta understood from later lines; from tat pratiṣṭhety upāsīta each meditation has its fruit: ‘as X meditate on that; one becomes X-vat’. Unit 4 ends with the identity statement sa yaś cāyaṃ puruṣe yaś cāsāv āditye sa ekaḥ. Unit 5 is one sentence: subject saḥ, five gerunds of passing (upasaṅkramya), a participle (anusañcaran), and the main verb āste with the participle gāyan; its object, etat sāma, is the chant that follows. Unit 6 is that chant, in the first person: nominal sentences (aham annam), a relative clause with its correlative (yo mā dadāti sa …), and the closing formula ya evaṃ veda, ity upaniṣat.

ambiguities.topic: suvar na jyotīḥ or suvarṇa jyotīḥ
ambiguities.note: The base text and the Sāyaṇa-pāṭha read सुवर्न ज्योतीः, which Śaṅkara explains as ‘a light like the sun’ («सुवः आदित्यः ; नकार उपमार्थे»). Madhva’s text, and the Viśiṣṭādvaita commentators, read सुवर्णज्योतीः, one compound: Kūranārāyaṇa ‘like the light called suvarṇa, the supreme abode’ («सुवर्णशब्दवाच्यं परमपदं»), Raṅgarāmānuja ‘with a lovely, shining body’ («कमनीयदेदीप्यमानशरीरः भवति»). The letters differ only in n against ṇ (and the space); corrections.json classifies Madhva’s reading as a variant. This edition keeps the base reading and gives both.

ambiguities.topic: Who is the ‘I’ of the song?
ambiguities.note: For Śaṅkara the knower who has become Brahman speaks as the one self of all («अद्वैत आत्मा निरञ्जनोऽपि सन् अहमेवान्नमन्नादश्च»). For Raṅgarāmānuja and Rāmānanda ‘I’ reaches to the supreme self who is the inner self of the speaker («अत्र अहं शब्दः परमात्मपर्यन्तः»). For Kūranārāyaṇa and Govindarāja the freed self speaks of itself as the Lord’s food and servant («अहमन्नं भगवतः भोग्यभूतः»).

Śaṅkara gives two senses at once: the three periods of life, and the three manners of giving, from respectful to grudging. Gopālānanda (modern) takes them as the best, middling and least food («मुख्यमध्यमाधमभेदेन»). Madhva reads the whole passage of the stage of life at which Brahman, called food, is realised, and what of him the freed soul then sees («मध्ये वयसि चेत् सिद्धं मुक्तो मध्यं प्रपश्यति»).

‘By whatever means.’ Rāmānanda limits it to the means proper to one’s station («तत्तद्वर्णविहितवृत्तिषु अन्यतमया वृत्त्या»); Kūranārāyaṇa’s gloss as printed reads ‘even by a forbidden means’ («प्रतिषिद्धेनापि»), which may be an OCR slip for ‘not forbidden’ and should be checked against the book.

Śaṅkara: the Brahman just named; Govindarāja: space, from the preceding sarvam ity ākāśe («सर्वत्र तच्छब्दात् आकाशम् उच्यते»). The parimara is the wind for Śaṅkara and Govindarāja (who cite a brāhmaṇa naming the five deities that die into it), and space for Raṅgarāmānuja.

ambiguities.topic: yo mā dadāti sa id eva mā3vāḥ
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: who gives me, food, to those who need it, preserves me («यः कश्चित् मा माम् अन्नमन्नार्थिभ्यो ददाति»). Raṅgarāmānuja and Rāmānanda: who teaches me to a fit pupil reaches me. Govindarāja: he who gave me [into being] has protected us both. The verb āvāḥ is read from av, ‘protect’, or from vā, ‘go’.

metre.name: prose
metre.note: Prose throughout. The chant of unit 6 is a sāman: its words are set with stobhas (hā3vu) and prolated vowels (annādo3, ṛtā3sya, nā3bhāyi, mā3vāḥ, ā3dmi, abhyabhavā3m), and with triple repetition, as sung, not as a metrical verse; the syllable counts shown on the page include these sung forms.

beginner: The last section of the Upaniṣad comes back to food. First, a rule for daily life: never turn away anyone who needs a place to stay, and keep enough food to feed them. Food given generously comes back generously; food given grudgingly comes back the same way. Then the teacher lists ordinary things — speech, breath, hands, feet, rain, lightning, cattle, stars, space — and asks the student to see the same deep reality at work in each. Finally the Upaniṣad pictures someone who has understood everything it taught. That person is so full of wonder that they burst into song: “I am food! I am the one who eats! I am the one who brings them together!” The song is strange on purpose. It is meant to show a mind that no longer feels separate from the world it once tried to grasp.
analogy: It is like the end of a long apprenticeship in a kitchen: the cook who began by fetching ingredients ends by seeing the meal, the eaters and the cooking as one occasion — and laughs.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Three things. A vow: never refuse anyone who comes for lodging, and so gather much food by any means; the knowers say to the guest, ‘food is ready for you’, and food returns to the giver in the manner it was given. A list of meditations: Brahman as keeping in speech, gaining-and-keeping in the breaths, action in the hands, movement in the feet, release in the organ of excretion; then in nature as satisfaction in rain, strength in lightning, fame in cattle, light in the stars, procreation, immortality and joy in the organ of generation, all in space; then as foundation, greatness, mind, homage, Brahman and ‘the dying-around of Brahman’, each with its fruit. And the knower: having passed through the five selves he moves through the worlds at will and sings the chant ‘I am food, I am the eater of food, I am the maker of the śloka; I am the first-born of the true order … I have overcome the whole world; my light is like the sun.’

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara links the vow to the meditation of the previous anuvāka, on earth and space as food and eater: one who meditates so must not turn a guest away («वसत्यर्थमागतं न निवारयेदित्यर्थः»), and since lodging implies a meal, must have food. He reads the three pairs as the return of a gift in kind: given in the first part of life or with full respect, food comes back so («मुख्ये प्रथमे वयसि मुख्यया वा वृत्त्या»). Kūranārāyaṇa extends the guest to anyone, ‘down to the outcaste’ («आचण्डालं»), and grounds it in the knower’s seeing the Lord in every self.

commentary.q: What are the meditations, and what do they give?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara defines the first two terms — keeping is guarding what one has («क्षेमो नाम उपात्तपरिरक्षणम्»), gaining is acquiring what one has not («योगः अनुपात्तस्योपादानम्») — and says that in each case it is Brahman that is to be meditated on under that form («ब्रह्म वाचि क्षेमरूपेण प्रतिष्ठितमित्युपास्यम्»). The fruit follows the form of the meditation, as a śruti he cites says: «तं यथा यथोपासते तदेव भवति». Raṅgarāmānuja names the same principle: «तत्क्रतुन्यायेन प्रतिष्ठादिकं भवति इत्यर्थः».

commentary.q: The person and the sun are one: why repeat it here?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara uses the line to close a long argument that the self which entered creation is the supreme self and does not transmigrate: «श्रुत्युपपत्तिभ्यां च सिद्धम् आत्मनोऽसंसारित्वम् , एकत्वाच्च». For Kūranārāyaṇa the person and the sun stand for the human and the divine, and ‘one’ means the one Lord over both («उभयत्र एकः एवेति»). Rāmānanda names that one as Śrī Rāma («परमात्मानं श्रीरामम्»).

commentary.q: What is the sāman, and why ‘hā3vu’?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: Brahman itself is the sāman because it is the same in all («समत्वाद्ब्रह्मैव साम»); the knower sings it to proclaim the oneness of the self and the fulfilment of his knowledge, and hā3vu is wonder, ‘aho!’ («अहो इत्येतस्मिन्नर्थेऽत्यन्तविस्मयख्यापनार्थम्»). Rāmānanda agrees that the syllables mean ‘aho’ and that prolation and threefold repetition mark extreme wonder («प्लुतत्वं त्रिरुच्चारणं च विस्मयातिशयख्यापनार्थम्»). Govindarāja has the freed soul sing it for as long as he remains («यावत्कालं तदेव साम पठति»).

commentary.q: Is release something to fear, if the released one becomes food?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara raises the objection himself: then I would fear liberation, since even freed I would be food for another. His answer is that food and eater belong to the world of transaction, which the knower has gone beyond; there is no second thing to fear, so release is not to be feared («अतो न भेतव्यं मोक्षात्»). The song praises the state of Brahman by speaking in the terms of that world.

commentary.q: How do the words of the chant work?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Several words appear in their sung forms: annādo3, ṛtā3sya, nā3bhāyi (nābhiḥ), mā3vāḥ, ā3dmi, abhyabhavā3m. The padaccheda keeps the sung forms where the prolation changes a vowel, and gives the pausal form where it does not (annādaḥ). suvar na uses the Vedic comparative na, ‘like’, which Śaṅkara names («नकार उपमार्थे»).

advaita.text: The knower passes beyond the five selves imagined by ignorance and attains the self that is real, knowledge, infinite, unborn, fearless and non-dual; he then moves through the worlds ‘as their self’, and his song is the joy of having nothing left to do. ‘I am food and the eater of food’ is said of the one self which is all: «अद्वैत आत्मा निरञ्जनोऽपि सन् अहमेवान्नमन्नादश्च». The two vallīs together are the Upaniṣad, knowledge of the supreme self («इति वल्लीद्वयविहिता उपनिषत् परमात्मज्ञानम्»).

visistadvaita.who: Kūranārāyaṇa; Raṅgarāmānuja; Bhāradvāja-Rāmānuja; Govindarāja; Rāmānanda; Gopālānanda (modern)
visistadvaita.text: The freed self reaches the self of bliss, the Lord, and remains distinct from him: Bhāradvāja draws the point from the gerunds and the participle — the released one stands apart from the supreme self, not having become one with it («परमात्मनः पृथक्त्वेन मुक्तपुरुषः स्थितः इत्युच्यते नत्त्वैक्यं प्राप्य»). Its song is the wonder of the servant who finds himself the Lord’s delight: Kūranārāyaṇa, «आत्मनः भगवद्भोग्यतां दृष्ट्वा तृप्त्यतिशयेन माद्यति»; Govindarāja makes the śloka-maker the Lord’s servant («श्लोककृत् पद्यकृत् दासभूतः इत्यर्थः»). Where the song says ‘I’, Raṅgarāmānuja reads it as reaching to the supreme self within the speaker («अत्र अहं शब्दः परमात्मपर्यन्तः»). The released one has a shining body: Raṅgarāmānuja «कमनीयदेदीप्यमानशरीरः भवति», Gopālānanda «कमनीयप्रकाशमानदिव्यरूपः भवति».

dvaita.ref: Taittirīyopaniṣad-bhāṣya, Bhṛguvallī 10, in verse (the imported text ends before the knower’s song)
dvaita.text: The vow is the knower’s: one who has come for learning or lodging is not to be refused («आगतं नेति न ब्रूयात् तदेतद् विदुषो व्रतम्»). The names in speech, breath, hands and so on are names of Hari dwelling there, each for the gift it gives («क्षेमकृत्वात् क्षेमनामा वाचिस्थः स परो हरिः»); and the ‘dying-around’ is Viṣṇu as destroyer even of Brahmā («विरिञ्चमारकश्चासौ ब्रह्म पूर्णगुणत्वतः»). The imported text of Madhva has nothing on the closing chant.

schools.disagreement: All agree that the knower passes through the five selves and sings. They disagree on what he has become: for Śaṅkara the one self, so that ‘I am food and the eater’ states identity with all; for the Viśiṣṭādvaita commentators a freed self, distinct from the Lord, whose ‘I’ either reaches to the Lord within or declares itself his food and servant; for Madhva every name in the list is a name of Viṣṇu. They also read the last words differently: ‘a light like the sun’ (Śaṅkara, with the base text) or ‘golden light’ (Madhva’s text and the Viśiṣṭādvaita commentators).

parallels.note: Śaṅkara reads this anuvāka as the explanation, left open in the Brahmānandavallī, of ‘he attains all desires together with Brahman’: what the desires are and how they are attained («‘सोऽश्नुते सर्वान्कामान्सह ब्रह्मणा विपश्चिता’ (तै. उ. २ । १ । १) इति तस्य फलवचनस्य अर्थविस्तारो नोक्तः»).
Cited by Kūranārāyaṇa and by Bhāradvāja for the freed one who moves through the worlds taking forms at will.

parallels.quote: यथाक्रतुरस्मिंल्लोके पुरुषो भवति तथेतः प्रेत्य भवति
parallels.note: Cited by Bhāradvāja for the passage through the selves: as one meditates here, so one becomes after death. The same principle underlies the list of meditations and their fruits.
Another first-person utterance of one who has realised Brahman (Vāmadeva); Bhāradvāja cites it, from its Ṛgvedic source, beside ‘I am food’.

contemporary.text: The vow at the end of the Upaniṣad is practical before it is mystical: keep enough to share, and do not send away the person at the door. Its claim that food returns in the manner it was given — generously or grudgingly — reads as a rule about character more than about reward: what we give shapes the kind of person who receives. The closing song then reverses ownership altogether. The one who knows does not say ‘I have food’ but ‘I am food’, as if the boundary between consumer and consumed had dissolved. In an economy built on that boundary, the image is worth sitting with. (A modern reflection, not the commentators’ reading.)

reflect.beginner: When someone needs help you could easily give, what usually makes you hesitate?
reflect.deeper: The song says ‘I am food and I am the eater of food’. In what sense might a person be both what is used and what uses?
reflect.practice: At one meal today, before eating, take a moment to recall where the food came from and who made it possible; then eat slowly, without a phone or a screen.

references.text: Śaṅkara’s comment includes, under 3.10.4, a long argument that the self which entered creation does not transmigrate; it is summarised above, not translated.

The six-commentary edition gives Raṅgarāmānuja, Govindarāja and Bhāradvāja on this anuvāka with their closing colophons; Govindarāja’s section also contains an editor’s footnote quoting Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara, and Bhāradvāja’s a footnote giving Śaṅkara’s reading suvar na jyotīḥ. Neither footnote is quoted here as the commentator’s.

flags.note: suvar na jyotīḥ (base, S, Śaṅkara) against suvarṇa jyotīḥ (Madhva’s text; read so by Kūranārāyaṇa, Raṅgarāmānuja, Govindarāja, Rāmānanda and Gopālānanda). See ambiguities and corrections.json.

The Sāyaṇa-pāṭha writes the pluti of annādo3 as ‘ऽ३ओ’, keeps the hiatus devebhyo amṛtasya, and keys lokān as लोकन् (a slip); Madhva’s text writes nābhāi for nābhāyi and spells the anusvāra as ग्ं. All are spelling or notation (corrections.json).
The sung forms nā3bhāyi and mā3vāḥ, and the form āvāḥ itself, are explained differently by every commentator; the word table gives Śaṅkara’s reading and notes the others.
Kūranārāyaṇa’s gloss on yayā kayā ca vidhayā reads «प्रतिषिद्धेनापि», ‘even by a forbidden [means]’, in the OCR text; it may be a misreading and should be checked against the printed edition.

Whether the knower of unit 5 passes through the selves into identity (Śaṅkara) or comes near to the self of bliss as to the Lord, remaining distinct (the Viśiṣṭādvaita commentators), is the main question of the anuvāka; the edition presents both.
